ethics_check.summary_text: All papers that appeared to involve live data collection contained an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All procedures were approved by the Vanderbilt University Institutional Review Board, and informed consent was obtained prior to participation.
Thirty participants (age 18-45 years; M = 23.3, SD = 6.6) were recruited through the Vanderbilt University SONA platform.
All procedures were approved by the Vanderbilt University Institutional Review Board, and informed consent was obtained prior to participation.
Participants were presented with lists of words and asked to remember these words.
During the presentation of the words, participants had to perform an encoding task, pressing the "F" or "J" key to indicate whether the word represented a smaller or larger object.
After each list, participants completed a 15 s integer addition task, generating sums of numbers chosen randomly from the range of 10 to 50.
Following the math distractor, participants were given 50 s to recall as many words as possible in any order by typing them into a text box and submitting with <enter>.
table.formatted: Following the math distractor, participants were given 50 s to recall as many words as possible in any order by typing them into a text box and submitting with <enter>.

table.text: In total, participants completed 16 trials, each consisting of a 20-word study list, a math distractor period, and a free recall period.
Response-key mappings for the encoding task were randomized across participants.
After each study phase, participants completed a 15-second distractor integer addition task, generating random sums of numbers between 10 and 50.
Before starting the main experiment, participants were exposed to a practice phase that taught them how to perform the experiment.
Across four practice lists, participants were gradually introduced to the semantic classification task, math distractor task, the free recall phase, and the two reward manipulations.
We examined the possibility that participants are not always successful in reinstating the start-of-list context by developing a mixture modeling approach to CMR.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

live_data_statements: Thirty participants (age 18-45 years; M = 23.3, SD = 6.6) were recruited through the Vanderbilt University SONA platform.
All procedures were approved by the Vanderbilt University Institutional Review Board, and informed consent was obtained prior to participation.
Participants were presented with lists of words and asked to remember these words.
During the presentation of the words, participants had to perform an encoding task, pressing the "F" or "J" key to indicate whether the word represented a smaller or larger object.
After each list, participants completed a 15 s integer addition task, generating sums of numbers chosen randomly from the range of 10 to 50.
Following the math distractor, participants were given 50 s to recall as many words as possible in any order by typing them into a text box and submitting with <enter>.
In total, participants completed 16 trials, each consisting of a 20-word study list, a math distractor period, and a free recall period.
Response-key mappings for the encoding task were randomized across participants.
After each study phase, participants completed a 15-second distractor integer addition task, generating random sums of numbers between 10 and 50.
Before starting the main experiment, participants were exposed to a practice phase that taught them how to perform the experiment.
Across four practice lists, participants were gradually introduced to the semantic classification task, math distractor task, the free recall phase, and the two reward manipulations.
We examined the possibility that participants are not always successful in reinstating the start-of-list context by developing a mixture modeling approach to CMR.
Participants were slower when the item was part of the high-reward sublist, but only for the rewarded recall condition (F(1,28) = 19.250, p < 0.001, η² p = 0.407).

The model revealed a significant effect of reward type (M = 1.993, HDI95% = [1.284, 2.824], pd = 1.000) indicating that participants were more likely to initiate recall with the first high-reward item in the rewarded recall condition than in the rewarded encoding condition.
After viewing these photographs, participants were tested for recognition memory, with some photographs being presented in the same sequential order as during encoding.
However, note that the participants were asked to remember the reward values of the photographs so that they could later select the most valuable ones.

In line with Karagoz et al. (2025), we observed that participants were slower and more error-prone at performing the semantic classification task for recall-rewarded items compared to encoding-rewarded items.

Both are hallmarks of serial recall, where participants are explicitly instructed to rehearse items in order, and there is ongoing debate about the extent to which serial recall and free recall rely on shared mechanisms, possibly involving rehearsal (Gunn & Polyn, 2025; Henson, 1998; Logan, 2021; Logan et al., 2021; Logan & Cox, 2021; Lohnas, 2024; Osth & Hurlstone, 2023; Solway et al., 2012; Tan & Ward, 2000; Ward et al., 2010; Ward & Beaman, 2025).

If this reflects rehearsal, and if participants had engaged in ongoing rehearsal of the mid-list rewarded items (positions 5-12), this should have also impaired performance on the concurrent encoding task for later items (13-20).
Similar arguments may hold for cued recall tasks, where participants are offered rewards for example for studying specific word pairs (De Loof et al., 2018).

text.text: Memory is an adaptive cognitive function that enables individuals to use past experiences to guide future behavior.

Prior research has demonstrated that goal-relevant, or rewarded, items are remembered more effectively, but the underlying mechanisms-ranging from neuromodulation of synaptic strength to increased semantic elaboration-remain debated.
In this study, we investigated how different reward structures influence the temporal organization of free recall in mixed-item lists.
Rewards were administered either during item encoding or were contingent on successful later recall.

Our behavioral results reveal a striking mid-list primacy effect: when rewards are contingent on later recall, participants disproportionately initiate search at the onset of rewarded subsequences, effectively treating reward shifts as privileged access points.
To account for these findings, we developed a novel hierarchical Bayesian implementation of the context maintenance and retrieval (CMR) model of free recall.
By fitting the model to individual recall sequences, we adjudicated between competing accounts of memory enhancement.
Our results demonstrate that motivated memory relies on two key mechanisms: the strengthening of context-to-item associations and the creation of accessible event boundaries.
These findings suggest the mid-list primacy effect involves the reinstatement of a privileged context rather than solely the enhanced encoding of early list items.
With regard to executive control and event segmentation theories, this suggests that participants exercise fine-grained control over their mental context, perhaps through various mnemonic techniques.
We propose that motivated memory is not merely a product of enhanced associative binding, but also involves active, structured (re)organization of experience.
Experiences carrying significance for future behavior are remembered more robustly than neutral ones.

A large body of work links the learning of goal-relevant information to a dopaminergic reinforcement learning system that promotes the learning of behaviorally relevant, rewarding experiences (Dolan & Dayan, 2013; Schultz, 2015).
text.formatted: A large body of work links the learning of goal-relevant information to a dopaminergic reinforcement learning system that promotes the learning of behaviorally relevant, rewarding experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Dolan & Dayan, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Schultz, 2015)</ref>.

text.text: However, reinforcement learning mechanisms typically rely on repeated exposure to reward before stable learning occurs (Niv, 2009; Sutton & Barto, 2018).
text.formatted: However, reinforcement learning mechanisms typically rely on repeated exposure to reward before stable learning occurs <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">(Niv, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">Sutton & Barto, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: By contrast, many adaptive decisions depend on remembering single episodes, a function that is served by the episodic memory system (Bornstein & Norman, 2017; Gershman & Daw, 2017).
text.formatted: By contrast, many adaptive decisions depend on remembering single episodes, a function that is served by the episodic memory system <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bornstein & Norman, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Gershman & Daw, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For the episodic memory system to contribute to adaptive behavior, it needs to preferentially encode and retrieve valuable information.

This may happen through two distinct routes-a more automatic process that strengthens memory in the presence of salient events, and a more strategic process that applies more effective encoding strategies when information is deemed important (Knowlton & Castel, 2022).
text.formatted: This may happen through two distinct routes-a more automatic process that strengthens memory in the presence of salient events, and a more strategic process that applies more effective encoding strategies when information is deemed important <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Knowlton & Castel, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we present experimental and computational evidence that people exercise fine-grained control over the temporal organization of memory when motivated by reward.

Reward modulation may occur via neuromodulatory signals that facilitate long-term potentiation in the hippocampus (Ergo et al., 2020; Miendlarzewska et al., 2016; Rouhani et al., 2023; Shohamy & Adcock, 2010).
text.formatted: Reward modulation may occur via neuromodulatory signals that facilitate long-term potentiation in the hippocampus <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Ergo et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">Miendlarzewska et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b76">Rouhani et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">Shohamy & Adcock, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: Behaviorally, this manifests as enhanced memory for items associated with reward anticipation or high incentive salience (Jang et al., 2019; Rouhani & Niv, 2021).
text.formatted: Behaviorally, this manifests as enhanced memory for items associated with reward anticipation or high incentive salience <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Jang et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Rouhani & Niv, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Beyond simple strengthening, these signals may influence the organization of memory by promoting event segmentation (Rouhani et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Beyond simple strengthening, these signals may influence the organization of memory by promoting event segmentation <ref type="bibr" target="#b74">(Rouhani et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, the release of norepinephrine in response to salient or surprising items can trigger event segmentation, signaling the end of one temporal unit and the start of another (Clewett et al., 2020; Nassar, 2024).
text.formatted: For instance, the release of norepinephrine in response to salient or surprising items can trigger event segmentation, signaling the end of one temporal unit and the start of another <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Clewett et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b63">Nassar, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Within these events, dopaminergic signaling may promote the integrative encoding of related stimuli (Clewett & Murty, 2019).
text.formatted: Within these events, dopaminergic signaling may promote the integrative encoding of related stimuli <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Clewett & Murty, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: These reward effects are typically demonstrated in recognition and paired-associate learning paradigms, where strong retrieval cues are provided at test, potentially masking the contribution of more strategic encoding and search processes that flexibly link value to memory organization.

In contrast, modulation of episodic memory organization has most often been examined in free recall paradigms, which place minimal constraints on retrieval cues and thus provide a sensitive window into the organization of memory.
Prioritization of high-value information often comes at the cost of low-value items.
In the value-directed remembering paradigm, recall probability increases with item value (Castel, 2007; Stefanidi et al., 2018).
text.formatted: In the value-directed remembering paradigm, recall probability increases with item value <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Castel, 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">Stefanidi et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: This effect has mainly been attributed to strategic processes, such as deeper semantic processing or the use of interactive imagery (Cohen et al., 2014; Knowlton & Castel, 2022).
text.formatted: This effect has mainly been attributed to strategic processes, such as deeper semantic processing or the use of interactive imagery <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Cohen et al., 2014;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Knowlton & Castel, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Notably, this effect disappears on "pure" lists where all items are either high or low value, suggesting that reward does not merely enhance memory globally but instead drives competitive dynamics during encoding or search (Talmi et al., 2021; see also Popov & Dames, 2023).
text.formatted: Notably, this effect disappears on "pure" lists where all items are either high or low value, suggesting that reward does not merely enhance memory globally but instead drives competitive dynamics during encoding or search <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Talmi et al., 2021</ref>; see also <ref type="bibr">Popov & Dames, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: These dynamics can be formally characterized within the retrieved context framework (Howard & Kahana, 2002), in which encoding involves binding items to a gradually evolving context representation, and retrieval proceeds by reinstating the context associated with recalled items, thereby guiding memory search along learned associations (Sederberg et al., 2008).
text.formatted: These dynamics can be formally characterized within the retrieved context framework <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Howard & Kahana, 2002)</ref>, in which encoding involves binding items to a gradually evolving context representation, and retrieval proceeds by reinstating the context associated with recalled items, thereby guiding memory search along learned associations <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Sederberg et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: By incorporating additional source information into the context (Polyn et al., 2009a) this can provide an explanation for why rewarded memoranda are preferentially recalled: reward signals may increase encoding strength or serve as a salient source cue that biases the search process (Horwath et al., 2023; Talmi et al., 2019 Talmi et al., , 2021)).
text.formatted: By incorporating additional source information into the context <ref type="bibr">(Polyn et al., 2009a)</ref> this can provide an explanation for why rewarded memoranda are preferentially recalled: reward signals may increase encoding strength or serve as a salient source cue that biases the search process <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Horwath et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Talmi et al., 2019</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">Talmi et al., , 2021))</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, it is not clear if these effects depend on whether memorization is instrumental for reward, or whether the saliency of rewarding information is itself sufficient to yield these effects.
Reward can also fundamentally reshape the initiation of memory search (Stefanidi et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Reward can also fundamentally reshape the initiation of memory search <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Stefanidi et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In standard free recall, participants typically exhibit a primacy effect: the tendency to recall initial list items first.
Originally, within the retrieved context framework, this was interpreted as enhanced encoding of early list items (Polyn et al., 2009a; Sederberg et al., 2008).
text.formatted: Originally, within the retrieved context framework, this was interpreted as enhanced encoding of early list items <ref type="bibr">(Polyn et al., 2009a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">Sederberg et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Alternative theories exist, for example emphasizing temporal distinctiveness of early list items (Brown et al., 2007).
text.formatted: Alternative theories exist, for example emphasizing temporal distinctiveness of early list items <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brown et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: However, there is increasing support for the idea that a dedicated start-of-list context representation can be formed during encoding, and reinstated at the start of the retrieval phase (Davelaar et al., 2005; Farrell, 2012; Healey & Wahlheim, 2024; Kragel et al., 2015; Lehman & Malmberg, 2013; Morton & Polyn, 2016; Osth & Farrell, 2019).
text.formatted: However, there is increasing support for the idea that a dedicated start-of-list context representation can be formed during encoding, and reinstated at the start of the retrieval phase <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Davelaar et al., 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Farrell, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Healey & Wahlheim, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">Kragel et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Lehman & Malmberg, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">Morton & Polyn, 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Osth & Farrell, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This mechanism is a cornerstone of models of short-term memory and related serial recall paradigms (Brown et al., 2000; Burgess & Hitch, 2005; Henson, 1998; Lewandowsky & Farrell, 2008; Lewandowsky & Murdock, 1989) providing a theoretical bridge between models of free recall and serial recall (Gunn & Polyn, 2025; Logan, 2021; Logan & Cox, 2021; Lohnas, 2024; Ward & Beaman, 2025).
text.formatted: This mechanism is a cornerstone of models of short-term memory and related serial recall paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Brown et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Burgess & Hitch, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Henson, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Lewandowsky & Farrell, 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Lewandowsky & Murdock, 1989)</ref> providing a theoretical bridge between models of free recall and serial recall <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gunn & Polyn, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Logan, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Logan & Cox, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Lohnas, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Ward & Beaman, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, from the perspective of retrieved context models, primacy initiation can be considered strategic.
Recall is most effective when it is initiated from the beginning of a studied list and proceeds forward-a strategy adopted by highly successful participants (Romani et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Recall is most effective when it is initiated from the beginning of a studied list and proceeds forward-a strategy adopted by highly successful participants <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">(Romani et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Zhang et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: This type of cueing is also effective in naturalistic memory, where experiences are organized into temporally persistent events separated by discrete boundaries that serve as access points, guiding retrieval of the associated episodes (Michelmann et al., 2023).
text.formatted: This type of cueing is also effective in naturalistic memory, where experiences are organized into temporally persistent events separated by discrete boundaries that serve as access points, guiding retrieval of the associated episodes <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">(Michelmann et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: We suggest that strategic encoding techniques, such as interactive imagery or story generation, can shape how events are formed and where boundaries are placed, allowing participants to structure recall and enhance accessibility-principles that could also govern the prioritization of high-value or rewarded items.
If primacy reflects the initiation of recall from a privileged context state, then such effects need not be restricted to the beginning of an entire list.
Instead, any segment of experience that is treated as a coherent and behaviorally relevant unit may function as a locally privileged starting point for memory search.

In this sense, sequences of items associated with reward may resemble the onset of an event, motivating participants to establish a new contextual anchor and to preferentially initiate retrieval from that point.
This predicts a mid-list primacy effect, in which recall disproportionately begins with the first item of a rewarded subsequence, even when that subsequence occurs in the middle of a longer list.

By fitting retrieved context models to recall sequences, we can directly compare whether these effects are better described by enhanced encoding or contextual control, informing the broader debate about whether primacy effects reflect encoding gradients or contextual reinstatement.
Importantly, reward can also be delivered in ways that are salient and affectively engaging without instrumentally depending on memorization of the related information.

To dissociate the effects of reward depending on successful memorization from more general effects of affective salience, we included a control condition in which participants received reward contingent on an immediate semantic classification of each item.
In this condition, reward cues remained visually salient and reliably predicted monetary outcomes, but reward itself did not instrumentally depend on memorization of the item.

From the perspective of retrieved context models, such a manipulation might produce salience-related effects on item processing that may manifest as a separate source context (Polyn et al., 2009a; Talmi et al., 2019) or a general increase in encoding strength (Horwath et al., 2023).
text.formatted: From the perspective of retrieved context models, such a manipulation might produce salience-related effects on item processing that may manifest as a separate source context <ref type="bibr">(Polyn et al., 2009a;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Talmi et al., 2019)</ref> or a general increase in encoding strength <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Horwath et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Comparing this condition to recall-contingent reward therefore allows us to test the degree to which changes in recall organization depend on an instrumental relationship between reward and successful memorization, rather than general reward-related salience or arousal.

Understanding these mechanisms is particularly important because age-related memory decline disproportionately affects automatic encoding processes, whereas older adults often retain the ability to exert strategic control over memory (Castel et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Understanding these mechanisms is particularly important because age-related memory decline disproportionately affects automatic encoding processes, whereas older adults often retain the ability to exert strategic control over memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Castel et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Identifying how reward and event structure interact with strategic control may reveal ways in which memory can be optimized despite overall reductions in encoding efficiency.

From this perspective, studying reward-induced mid-list primacy and context reinstatement provides insight not only into fundamental mechanisms of memory organization, but also into potential avenues for mitigating memory decline.
The aims of the current paper are twofold.
First, while prior work suggests that sourcecontext organization is a primary mechanism for reward-driven memory, we propose that this is not the only route (see also Horwath et al., 2023).
text.formatted: First, while prior work suggests that sourcecontext organization is a primary mechanism for reward-driven memory, we propose that this is not the only route (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Horwath et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: By simulating control over contextual anchoring and recall initiation, we aim to show that memory organization is highly flexible, allowing participants to exploit environmental structure in service of goal-directed retrieval.

More generally, we use our reward manipulation to inform a fundamental debate regarding the nature of the primacy effect as modeled within the retrieved context framework: is it driven by forming stronger associations for early list items during encoding, or do participants explicitly search for early list items when initiating recall?
By analyzing recall sequences with retrieved context models, we use reward-induced mid-list primacy to distinguish between these competing mechanisms.

Our results provide strong evidence for mid-list primacy for retrieval-contingent reward, best explained by tab divider-like markers in temporal context, enabling later recall to be guided according to these markers.
Furthermore, we find that overall recall improvements also reflect encoding enhancements and source-context organization, conceptually replicating and extending earlier work.

text.text: Thirty participants (age 18-45 years; M = 23.3, SD = 6.6) were recruited through the Vanderbilt University SONA platform.

text.text: Participants received $20/hour plus up to an additional $10 per session based on task performance, with compensation provided in the form of Amazon gift cards.
One participant was excluded for failing to comply with task instructions (not completing the distractor math problems between encoding and retrieval), leaving a final sample of 29 for analysis.
Participants were presented with lists of words and asked to remember these words.
The words were drawn without replacement from a pool of 624 items that had been unanimously rated by a separate group as either smaller or larger than a shoebox (Diachek et al., 2023).

Participants could type the answer into a text box and submit their answer with the <enter> key.

text.text: Task performance was rewarded.
Participants could earn points, with every 10 points corresponding to $0.05 bonus payment at the end of the experiment.

Participants always earned at least one point for correctly performing the encoding task on each word at study, one point for every correctly solved math problem, and one point for recalling each word at test.
In total, participants completed 16 trials, each consisting of a 20-word study list, a math distractor period, and a free recall period.
For each list, we manipulated the reward contingencies so that some study words would earn 10 points rather than only 1 point (Fig 1A).

text.text: These increased rewards were offered in contiguous sublists.
These high-reward words could be present in the middle of the list (the middle sublist; items 5-12), or at the end of the list (the end sublist; items 13-20).
The first four words were considered a burn-in sequence and were never associated with the higher reward.

Two reward conditions existed, with the rewarded encoding condition (Fig. 1A, magenta) offering 10 points for correctly classifying the word as small or large, and the rewarded recall condition (Fig. 1A, blue) offering 10 points for recalling the word during the free recall period.

text.text: This yielded four list types, each shown four times across the experiment for every participant in a fully randomized order.
To control potential order effects, we balanced the encoding task responses across and within sublists.
Each correct response appeared equally often and was equally likely to be preceded by the same or the alternate response, for each serial position.
This avoided systematic effects of response alternation, which are known to slow reaction times and potentially influence encoding.
Four possible response sequences were created (Fig. 1B), and each list type was paired once with each sequence.

During the main experiment, participants could take self-paced breaks after each recall phase.
At the end of the experiment, the experimenter asked participants whether they found any part of the task particularly difficult or used any memory strategies.
Participants responded verbally, and the experimenter took written notes.
The full session lasted approximately 60 minutes.

We implemented a hierarchical Bayesian version of CMR in Stan (Carpenter et al., 2017) and considered three possible reward mechanisms: A general enhancement of associative strength for rewarded items, the construction of a separate reward source, and the formation of accessible event boundaries for the rewarded sublist.

text.text: The input layer f is a representational space allowing for the activation of localist codes for each study item as it is encountered on the list.

text.text: This input layer projects to a context (hidden) layer c.
Pre-existing associations link each featural element to a corresponding contextual element.

The context layer additionally includes various representations of organizational features that can aid memory search, including start-of-list context (which is activated before the first study item is presented) and rewardrelated source features (which are activated for low-reward and high-reward items, respectively).
An item-to-context weight matrix ( 𝐌 ) projects from f to c, allowing feature activation to influence the contextual representation.
A context-to-item weight matrix (𝐌 ), projects from c back to f, allowing for the reactivation of feature representations during the recall phase.
These memory activations of the study items are conceptualized as an output layer (𝐟 ), not depicted in the schematic figure.
Learning is simulated as the formation of bidirectional Hebbian associations between items and context, on these weight matrices.

text.text: We examined the possibility that participants are not always successful in reinstating the start-of-list context by developing a mixture modeling approach to CMR.
On a subset of trials (whose proportion is estimated with the free parameter 𝑝 ) the model operates in primacy mode, in which start-of-list context is reactivated.
On the rest of the trials, it operates in a recency mode, and no such reinstatement takes place.
The temporal organization between these modes is hypothesized to differ, with the primacy mode emphasizing forward recall and the recency mode emphasizing backwards recall (Zhang et al., 2023).

text.text: We allowed certain model parameters to take on distinct values in primacy mode and recency mode.

We also allowed a distinct degree of retrieved experimental context during the recall phase, controlled by 𝛾 and 𝛾 parameters.
During model fitting, we compute the likelihood of each recall sequence under each of these two modes and weight their likelihoods using the mixture parameter 𝑝.
We consider three possible reward-sensitive mechanisms within CMR (see Fig. 3).

text.text: The first mechanism is a reward-sensitive modified attention gradient.
This mechanism causes a sharp increase in the strength of context-to-item associations (ϕ) upon presentation of the first rewarded item.
The scale of the increase, the rate of its decay, and its asymptotic value are controlled respectively by the parameters 𝜙 , 𝜙 , and 𝜙.
The second mechanism introduces reward source elements into the contextual representation, implemented by creating a reward-incentive state context sub-layer in c.
This source layer has 2 units.

The low-incentive unit (small dollar sign, Fig. 2) is 1 during the presentation of low-reward words and 0 during the presentation of high-reward words, and vice versa for the high-incentive unit (large dollar sign, Fig. 2).

The third mechanism introduces contextual control and can alter the way recall is initiated.
Rather than having a primacy mode where the start-of-list context is reactivated and a recency mode where it is not, we allow a primacy-recency mode and a reward targeting mode.

The primacy-recency mode reflects the standard operation of CMR, where the model parameters determine the relative strength of start-of-list and end-of-list context in guiding memory search (resembling earlier implementations of CMR that used start-of-list reinstatement without a mixture implementation; Kragel et al., 2015; Morton & Polyn, 2016; Healey & Wahlheim, 2024).

In this model variant, the primacy-recency mode and the reward-targeting mode each have distinct 𝛽 and 𝛾 parameters, to account for potential differences in temporal organization between the two modes.

A future model may consider a mixture implementation with 3 separate primacy, recency, and reward targeting modes, however we found the binary mixture described above to provide adequate fits to initiation effects while helping to control model complexity.
In this model variant, the 𝑝 parameter is used to control the mixture of reward-targeting mode and primacyrecency mode (1-𝑝 ).
Importantly, these three mechanisms-the modified attention gradient, reward source, and contextual control-are not treated as mutually exclusive.

text.text: Participants encountered different lists that manipulated i) the type of reward that was available-either for correctly performing a semantic encoding task or for successful later recall, and ii) the list positions in which this reward was available-either the middle (items 5-12) or the end (items 13-20) of the list.
We found large differences in performance based on the reward type and its' position in the list.
Participants performed the encoding task with high accuracy, but were slower and less accurate when encoding recall-rewarded items.
Recall-rewarded items were recalled much more often compared to non-rewarded or encoding-rewarded items, and demonstrated enhanced temporal organization.
Participants tended to initiate recall with the first recall-rewarded item, which proved highly constraining to the set of computational models we examined.
In the results sections below, we present the posterior predictions of the best-fitting model alongside the empirical results.

Performance on the binary semantic classification task was disrupted in the rewarded recall condition, possibly reflecting the engagement of cognitive processes to enhance the memorability of items.

This is consistent with the engagement of executive processes to enhance the memorability of recall-rewarded words, at the cost of fast encoding task performance.

Note that we also conducted single-trial regression models of response times yielding identical results, but these models showed substantial misspecification and are therefore only reported in Appendix B.
It is possible that the high-priority study items from the rewarded recall condition could receive special treatment in the form of continuing rehearsal (Brodie & Murdock, 1977; Tan & Ward, 2000).

text.text: We examined this possibility with a second set of analyses of classification performance.
Continued rehearsal of (recall-rewarded) items adds a cognitive load to the participant which should disrupt task performance beyond the classification of the item itself.

We compared response times in the end sublist when the middle sublist had high rewards, and did not find slower response times for these items in the rewarded recall condition relative to the rewarded encoding condition (F(1,28) = 0.020, p = 0.888, η² p < 0.001).

text.text: This suggests that enhanced recall of high-reward words in the middle of the list is not due to rehearsal of those words, which would have interfered with task performance for low-rewarded words occurring at the end of the list.
A complementary set of analyses demonstrated that accuracy effects mirrored latency effects.
Single-trial regression modeling provided a good fit for these data (see Appendix B for full model specification and posterior predictive check).

We observed a similar three-way interaction between sublist location, reward location, and reward type (M = -1.344, HDI95% = [-2.245, -0.454], pd = 0.999): participants made more errors for high reward words in the rewarded recall condition than in the rewarded encoding condition.
In order to determine whether continuing rehearsal could affect task accuracy, we carried out an analogous analysis to the latency analysis described above.

Testing the accuracy in the end sublist when the middle sublist had high rewards again did not reveal a significant difference between the rewarded encoding and recall conditions (M = -0.232, HDI95% = [-0.708, 0.219], pd = 0.840) again not showing evidence in favor of continuing rehearsal processes.
The memorability of individual items was enhanced in the rewarded recall condition, specifically for the subset of rewarded items.

We characterized these effects with a single-trial logistic regression model on the probability of recalling each word, using the same three factors as for the encoding task performance-reward condition, reward location, and sublist membership.
Single-trial regression modeling provided a good fit for these data (see Appendix B for full model specification and posterior predictive checks).
Participants recalled more items overall in the rewarded recall condition than in the rewarded encoding condition (M = 0.261, HDI95% = [0.114, 0.399], pd = 1.000).
Recall was also generally higher for the end sublist than for the middle sublist (M = 0.181, HDI95% = [0.048, 0.321], pd = 0.995).
Importantly, recall was enhanced specifically in the high-reward sublist, regardless of its position in the list (M = 1.356, HDI95% = [1.002, 1.712], pd = 1.000).

This reward-location effect was further qualified by a threeway interaction, such that the advantage for high-reward sublists was substantially larger in the rewarded recall condition than in the rewarded encoding condition (M = 2.157, HDI95% = [1.419, 2.852], pd = 1.000).
These memorability effects can be seen in more detail in the serial position curves for each of the list types (Fig. 5).

We characterized reward-related effects on the temporal organization scores with a repeatedmeasures ANOVA, with high-vs. low reward items and reward condition (rewarded encoding vs. rewarded recall) as factors, collapsing across middle vs. end sublist position.
This analysis revealed that high reward items showed stronger temporal organization than low reward items (F(1,28) = 10.500, p = 0.003, η² p = 0.273).
The rewarded recall condition also showed stronger temporal organization overall compared to the rewarded encoding condition (F(1,28) = 9.011, p = 0.006, η² p = 0.243).
Importantly, these effects interacted.
Temporal organization was particularly enhanced for high reward items when recall rewards were at stake (F(1,28) = 9.860, p = 0.004, η² p = 0.260).
A similar analysis was applied to the forward asymmetry measure.
Here the ANOVA showed a reliable effect of reward, with high reward items exhibiting stronger forward asymmetry than low reward items (F(1,28) = 12.493, p = 0.001, η² p = 0.309).
However, there was no significant difference between the rewarded encoding and rewarded recall conditions.

text.text: By comparing these models' posterior predictive distributions with observed behavior, we can adjudicate which qualitative features of motivated memory depend on each specific mechanism in more detail than through integral model comparison or contrasts of isolated parameter values (see Appendix C for an analysis including only a single reward mechanism at a time).

An examination of the serial position curves generated by these reduced models shows that certain qualitative features of the serial position curves-a sharp increase at reward onset followed by a gradual decay-can be reproduced regardless of removing any single mechanism.

However, a closer examination reveals that without the modified attention gradient, the model can capture the performance enhancement for the middle sublist for recall-rewarded items, but cannot capture this enhancement for the first several rewarded items in the end sublist.
The reason for this failure is because of an interaction between the recency effect and the enhanced associations formed in the source context through the RLR parameter.

When recall rewards appear in the end sublist, the last few items and the high-reward source context remain somewhat in contextual focus (despite our math distractor task and the associated parameter βdistraction).
This yields increased competition with the early reward items in the end sublist.

This competition from recent items is decreased when recall rewards appear in the middle sublist, because both the later reward items as well as the high-reward source have been replaced in the context by the lower-reward end sublist.

Including the attention gradient avoids this problem, as the stronger associations for early reward items resolve the competition from recent items when rewards are present in the end sublist.  5) for the rewarded recall condition, grouped by whether the rewards were present in the middle sublist (top row) or end sublist (bottom row).

Overall, this indicates that contextual control is responsible for establishing the tight forward organization of recall, while the modified attention gradient determines the relative strength of the underlying memories.
Only when both mechanisms are present do the posterior predictions reproduce the sharply ordered recall structure observed in the rewarded recall condition.
Memory is essential for daily functioning, yet our cognitive resources are finite.
We must prioritize information that is most relevant for future behavior.

In this work, we investigated the architecture of this prioritization, asking whether motivated memory is driven by processes such as the strengthening of memory traces, perhaps through neuromodulation, or by control over the mental context that can be used to search for specific information later on.

By comparing rewards administered during encoding with those contingent on later recall, we observed that while simple reward salience provides a modest boost to memorability, the structure of memory is more fundamentally reorganized when memorization is instrumental to obtaining reward.

Recall-based rewards, but not encoding-task rewards, produced highly structured free recall response sequences, with participants preferentially initiating recall at the beginning of the rewarded subsequence and then recalling items in forward order.
We created a family of models incorporating three theoretically dominant reward-based mechanisms expressed within the Context Maintenance and Retrieval framework (CMR; Polyn et al., 2009a).

Nevertheless, we observed a much stronger effect of the attention gradient when rewards were contingent on later recall compared to semantic classification performance, indicating a strong dependence on memorization being instrumental for reward acquisition.

text.text: Nevertheless, our simulations also demonstrated that the attention gradient mechanism is not sufficient to explain the effect of reward on recall initiation.
Participants showed a strong preference for initiating recall specifically with the first recall-rewarded item, that could not be captured solely by an increase in overall memorability for this item.
We demonstrated that the reward source mechanism was not responsible for any of the qualitative organization features observed in the rewarded recall condition.

When rewarded items are interspersed randomly throughout the list, participants still tend to cluster these items together during free recall-an organizational feature that can be captured by such a separate reward context guiding memory search (Horwath et al., 2023; Talmi et al., 2021).

Our model comparison still indicated that the reward source mechanism helps to improve the overall model fit of CMR to the empirical data, possibly by enhancing the overall contrast in memorability between high-reward items and low-reward items, while the attention gradient and the contextual control mechanisms emphasize differences in memorability within the rewarded subsequence.
We observed small effects on overall memorability and recall initiation in the rewarded encoding condition.
Such effects have been observed in other free recall tasks as well.
For example, Polyn et al. (2009b) asked participants to make semantic judgments during encoding, either size (smaller/larger than a basketball) or animacy (animate/inanimate).

text.text: Several consecutive items required the same judgment before switching to the other task within a single list.

At recall, participants tended to cluster items by judgment type and, importantly, showed a small but reliable increase in the probability of recalling the first post-switch item early, including as the first recall, resembling the results in our rewarded encoding condition.
They were able to model these effects with a source context representing the task that had to be performed for each item.

However, in our reward encoding condition participants occasionally may have engaged the same memorization processes as they may have used for recall-rewarded items, resulting in these signatures reflecting sporadic trials in which a stronger reward-modified attention gradient or contextual control mechanism would have operated.

text.text: By manipulating the reward type, we demonstrated that reward motivation can enhance the segmentation of these events, as well as the integration of items within a single event.

Participants initiated recall at the event boundary more consistently, as well as forming stronger context-to-item associations, specifically when they could receive rewards for later recall of the items.

Our results expand on other recent approaches that investigated the effect of reward prediction errors on event segmentation. Rouhani et al. (2020) asked participants to view photographs associated with various levels of reward, and to remember the reward values associated with each photograph so they could later select the most valuable ones.

text.text: Reward levels were clustered in time, meaning that photographs associated with relatively high reward values all followed each other, and were clearly separate from photographs associated with lower reward values.
After viewing these photographs, participants were tested for recognition memory, with some photographs being presented in the same sequential order as during encoding.
This revealed sequential probing effects on recognition memory, where recognition memory performance is faster for photographs that were presented in the same sequential order as during encoding.

Crucially, this effect was diminished for photographs that spanned an event boundary-specifically the items before and after a change in the mean reward value, excluding the first item of the new reward value.
This was interpreted as evidence that reward prediction errors provide the crucial signal to trigger event segmentation.
However, note that the participants were asked to remember the reward values of the photographs so that they could later select the most valuable ones.
We demonstrated that our signature of event segmentation, the mid-list primacy effect, mainly affects such recall-rewarded items.

Overall, this suggests that the increased engagement of contextual control and attention gradient mechanisms in the rewarded recall condition may be strategic.

text.text: This suggests the engagement of capacity-limited cognitive processes to enhance the memorability of these items, at the cost of encoding task performance.
These cognitive processes may take the form of participants coming up with a story involving the words as they appear, or placing the items together in a visual scene.
Indeed, in the post-experiment interview, 17 out of 29 participants reported using strategies such as imagining a story that linked the words together or placing the words in a visual scene.
Application of such strategies has previously been argued to result in primacy initiation and forward organization (Romani et al., 2016; Zhang et al., 2023).

text.text: Such rich and long-form content would yield substantial interference if all details were equally committed to memory, resulting in ineffective memory search when specific content needs to be remembered later on.

Event segmentation processes provide a crucial preprocessing step during (or shortly after) encoding, identifying what parts are important to remember and the best way to commit these to memory, in order to minimize such interference.

Our results demonstrate that similar processes can occur in a more artificial setting such as learning lists of arbitrary words, and appear under strategic control when reward acquisition is dependent on successful recall.
This provides a novel and simplified experimental technique for investigating the role of cognitive control in memory encoding and retrieval.

Future work may further characterize the computations involved in deciding when and how to form these event representations, for example by combining the architecture of CMR with reinforcement learning algorithms that can learn to control (particular dimensions of) the context layer.
If such event segmentation processes help enhance memory performance, why do participants not always employ them in typical free recall tasks where the goal is to remember as many words as possible?
One potential answer can be found in the literature on cognitive control.
Better performance in cognitive tasks often comes with a perceived cost of exerting cognitive effort (Shenhav et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Better performance in cognitive tasks often comes with a perceived cost of exerting cognitive effort <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">(Shenhav et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Participants may not be willing to exert such effort, unless substantial rewards are contingent on it.
Nevertheless, participants may occasionally employ such processes spontaneously.
Indeed, Zhang et al. (2023) found that the best participants in a free recall task tend to show primacy initiation and forward organization (see also Romani et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Indeed, <ref type="bibr" target="#b102">Zhang et al. (2023)</ref> found that the best participants in a free recall task tend to show primacy initiation and forward organization (see also <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Romani et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: More generally, Farrell (2012) demonstrated that associations in memory may often cluster together in shorter chunks, which are accessed from the first item and recalled in a forward order.
text.formatted: More generally, <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Farrell (2012)</ref> demonstrated that associations in memory may often cluster together in shorter chunks, which are accessed from the first item and recalled in a forward order.

text.text: Such chunks may reflect the participant identifying richer relationships between these items, possibly through similar forms of imagery as we proposed play a role in generating the mid-list primacy effect.
We must consider the possibility that other executive mechanisms not considered here could also account for these behavioral effects.

For example, there is a substantial literature linking both primacy initiation and forward organization to rehearsal strategies in which studied items are repeated covertly by the participant throughout the list (Brodie & Murdock, 1977; Laming, 2006).
text.formatted: For example, there is a substantial literature linking both primacy initiation and forward organization to rehearsal strategies in which studied items are repeated covertly by the participant throughout the list <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Brodie & Murdock, 1977;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Laming, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Both are hallmarks of serial recall, where participants are explicitly instructed to rehearse items in order, and there is ongoing debate about the extent to which serial recall and free recall rely on shared mechanisms, possibly involving rehearsal (Gunn & Polyn, 2025; Henson, 1998; Logan, 2021; Logan et al., 2021; Logan & Cox, 2021; Lohnas, 2024; Osth & Hurlstone, 2023; Solway et al., 2012; Tan & Ward, 2000; Ward et al., 2010; Ward & Beaman, 2025).
text.formatted: Both are hallmarks of serial recall, where participants are explicitly instructed to rehearse items in order, and there is ongoing debate about the extent to which serial recall and free recall rely on shared mechanisms, possibly involving rehearsal <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Gunn & Polyn, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Henson, 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b51">Logan, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Logan et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Logan & Cox, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b54">Lohnas, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b66">Osth & Hurlstone, 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Solway et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">Tan & Ward, 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b99">Ward et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b98">Ward & Beaman, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In our experiment, one might argue that the rewarded recall condition encouraged participants to rehearse the rewarded items in sequence, thereby producing primacy initiation and forward transitions.
However, several observations argue against this interpretation.

In the post-experiment interview, only six participants reported attempting rehearsal strategies, and two of these noted that they switched from rehearsal to a story/scene strategy later in the task, finding the latter more effective.
Most participants thus did not admit relying on rehearsal, and among the six who reported attempting it, two spontaneously described it as inefficient.
Second, we observed that recall rewards impair performance on the encoding task.

If this reflects rehearsal, and if participants had engaged in ongoing rehearsal of the mid-list rewarded items (positions 5-12), this should have also impaired performance on the concurrent encoding task for later items (13-20).
Instead, we observed no such persistent slowdown or accuracy cost, suggesting that participants did not continue rehearsing reward items into the remainder of the list.
Therefore, while rehearsal could in principle generate similar organizational signatures, we believe it is unlikely to account for our results.

Instead, the CMR framework provides a more parsimonious explanation, attributing primacy initiation and forward organization to the joint influence of enhanced context-to-item encoding and contextual control.
Beyond the influence of rehearsal, other mechanisms have been invoked to explain the primacy effect.
It has been suggested that the early list items have a higher temporal distinctiveness and are therefore more salient and better encoded (Brown et al., 2007).
text.formatted: It has been suggested that the early list items have a higher temporal distinctiveness and are therefore more salient and better encoded <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Brown et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: Our midlist primacy effect demonstrates strong primacy-like effects can exist regardless of temporal distinctiveness, likely involving some form of strategic control over event segmentation and item processing.
In this sense, we have demonstrated that such processes may play a role in generating the canonical primacy effect.
However, we did not rule out that other factors such as temporal distinctiveness may play a role in generating the canonical primacy effect, in addition to the strategic processes we proposed.
Future experiments may further characterize the nature of the mid-list primacy effect and its relation to the canonical primacy effect.
For example, it is not known what would happen if recall-rewards would be present from the first item onward.
Strategic processes as we proposed may further increase the strength of the primacy effect by increasing the chance or strength of the contextual reinstatement process.
This may overwrite original primacy generating processes, add to them, or these processes might interact in some way.

Additionally, participants in our design may have realized that the absence of rewards in the middle of a list predicts the presence of rewards at the end of that list, allowing them to prepare in advance for the onset of these rewards.

More generally, the fixed and repeating nature of the reward sequences in our experiment would diminish influences from surprise, salience, or reward prediction error that may contribute to mid-list primacy effects.
Nevertheless, we found this effect to be strongly present in both in middle-and end-reward lists.
This is easier explained by potentially strategic processes, rather than effects of surprise, salience, or prediction error.
We additionally investigated whether the mid-list primacy effects change between the first and last experimental half.
If surprise, salience, or prediction error contributes more to these effects, they should be stronger in the first half, while strategic effects may become more reliable in the latter half.
However, we did not find any such difference between early and late experimental halves.
Our design focused on investigating memory organization through free recall.
Other reward effects have been studied using recognition memory (Jang et al., 2019; Rouhani et al., 2018; Rouhani & Niv, 2021).
text.formatted: Other reward effects have been studied using recognition memory <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Jang et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Rouhani et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Rouhani & Niv, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: There, prediction errors often yield improved memory for items that were more surprising, even when the rewards are administered independent of later memory for the related items.
The weak effects of such encoding rewards in our paradigm can be understood in two ways.
First of all, as highlighted above, the predictability of our design may have attenuated the effect of prediction errors.

Alternatively, encoding rewards may serve to make the items themselves more salient and therefore better encoded, but do not encourage the strategic processes we have emphasized that enhance the item-to-context binding strength.

The increased saliency of individual items may make them more recognizable when the exact item is encountered later on, without making items more effective at cueing memory for other items on the list.
Similar arguments may hold for cued recall tasks, where participants are offered rewards for example for studying specific word pairs (De Loof et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Similar arguments may hold for cued recall tasks, where participants are offered rewards for example for studying specific word pairs <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(De Loof et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: These rewards encourage the formation of associations between the relevant items within a pair, but would not increase the efficacy with which words across different pairs would cue each other during recall.

While CMR is classically applied to free recall, recent work has extended this to recognition and cued recall paradigms (Polyn & Woodman, 2025), although this work did not incorporate reward effects into the model.
text.formatted: While CMR is classically applied to free recall, recent work has extended this to recognition and cued recall paradigms <ref type="bibr" target="#b70">(Polyn & Woodman, 2025)</ref>, although this work did not incorporate reward effects into the model.

text.text: The original formulation of CMR included an exponentially decaying attention gradient, which is limited in generality.
In value-directed remembering paradigms, items are often assigned unique point values that are randomly interspersed within a list.
Recall probability typically scales with these point values, a graded effect that a uniformly decaying attention gradient cannot reproduce.
A more flexible framework, such as the one from Ma et al. (2026) discussed above, would address this gap.
text.formatted: A more flexible framework, such as the one from <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Ma et al. (2026)</ref> discussed above, would address this gap.

text.text: It may be possible to implement such value-based encoding mechanisms within CMR, supplanting the attention gradient mechanism and providing a more general account for the primacy effect as well as the value-based memory effects.

Our implementation of contextual control was likewise deliberately constrained to align with our experimental task by only considering event segmentation specifically when changing between high and low rewards, which simplified hierarchical Bayesian model fitting and comparison.
The CMR model is a simplified form of a recurrent neural network using linear associative connections and a simple integration mechanism.

This makes it part of a broader lineage of recurrent neural networks; training such a network with backpropagation has been shown to reproduce a wide range of complex memory-related phenomena (Botvinick & Plaut, 2006; Botvinick & Plaut, 2004; Elman, 1990; Franklin et al., 2020; Gershman et al., 2025; Holroyd et al., 2018; Jensen et al., 2024; Li et al., 2026; Lu et al., 2022; Shahnazian & Holroyd, 2018; Wang et al., 2018).
text.formatted: This makes it part of a broader lineage of recurrent neural networks; training such a network with backpropagation has been shown to reproduce a wide range of complex memory-related phenomena <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Botvinick & Plaut, 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Botvinick & Plaut, 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Elman, 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Franklin et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Gershman et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Holroyd et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Jensen et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">Li et al., 2026;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">Lu et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Shahnazian & Holroyd, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b96">Wang et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: From this perspective, contextual control could take more flexible forms, dynamically shaping both encoding and retrieval according to task demands.
However, the strength of these neural-network approaches-capturing behavior through optimized distributed representations-is also their limitation.
They do not afford explicit likelihood-based fitting, and therefore cannot provide the same statistical interpretability that our constrained CMR extensions allow.
Our findings highlight CMR as a uniquely powerful framework for modeling how rewards shape episodic memory.

By formalizing both enhanced context-to-item binding (via the modified attention gradient) and the manipulation of mental context during encoding and retrieval (via contextual control), CMR enables direct tests of competing hypotheses about encoding strategies and recall organization and revealed their unique, nuanced contributions.
Crucially, CMR allows for explicit likelihood-based model comparison, making it especially well-suited for adjudicating between mechanisms that can produce similar behavior.

Looking forward, reward-augmented extensions of CMR provide a promising foundation for integrating neural and behavioral data (Kragel et al., 2015; Nunez et al., 2024; Polyn, 2024; Turner et al., 2017).
text.formatted: Looking forward, reward-augmented extensions of CMR provide a promising foundation for integrating neural and behavioral data <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Kragel et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b65">Nunez et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">Polyn, 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b93">Turner et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Such approaches could help identify neural signatures not only of strengthened context-to-item associations (cf. Ma et al., 2025) but also of the contextual control processes we considered here, advancing our understanding of how motivation organizes memory for rewarding experiences, and the primacy effect in general.

Fig 3 Reward mechanisms in CMR.
(A) Typically, CMR has an attention gradient: a decaying learning rate for context-to-item associations.
(B) We test a model mechanism which engages a modified attention gradient when high rewards are available (represented by the colored line for mid-list items).
(C) In a standard free-recall experiment, incentive state is not manipulated, making it unnecessary to explicitly include a representation of incentive context.
(D) The experimental manipulation of reward may elicit distinct incentive contexts for the different study items, justifying the explicit simulation of this source feature.
If the source feature is active during search, the memories associated with that source feature will receive extra support.
(E) Typically, participants initiate recall with a blend of start-of-list context (supporting primacy effects) and end-of-list context (supporting recency effects).
(F) The shift from low-reward to high-reward items may trigger the formation of a unique contextual feature representing an event boundary during encoding (indicated by the gate icon).
Reactivating this event boundary context during recall initiation would provide another place in the list to initiate recall.FunctionParameter Range Description
